summary: Describes how OSPFv3 can carry multiple address families by running multiple instances, mapping each family to an instance using the Instance ID field in the packet header. It is a proposed standard and needs few changes to OSPFv3.

eli5.summary: Instead of building a new road map for each kind of address, you run one map for each kind, labeled with a number.

questions: what is the ospfv3 af bit
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routes IPv4 and multicast prefixes by running one separate OSPFv3 instance per address family.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 was defined for IPv6 unicast only, but networks also need to advertise multicast IPv6, unicast IPv4 and multicast IPv4 routes.
tldr.mechanism: Each address family is mapped to its own range of Instance IDs, and each Instance ID is a separate OSPFv3 instance with its own neighbors, link state database and SPF calculation. A new AF-bit in the Options field keeps unaware routers from forming adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: Multiple address families work with few changes to OSPFv3 and can be deployed gradually. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 6969, RFC 7949, RFC 8362 and RFC 9454.

today: RFC 5838 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6969, RFC 7949, RFC 8362 and RFC 9454. It builds on OSPFv3 as defined in RFC 5340.

sections.title: Why Use Multiple Instances
sections.content:
OSPFv3, defined in RFC 5340, supports the base IPv6 unicast address family (AF). There are requirements to advertise other AFs as well: multicast IPv6, unicast IPv4 and multicast IPv4. This document supports them by mapping each AF to a separate Instance ID and OSPFv3 instance.

The RFC gives its reasons. OSPFv3 already supports multiple instances, so mapping an instance to an AF adds no new mechanism, minimizes protocol extensions and simplifies implementations. A separate link state database per AF is also easier to debug and operate, and the existing instance, area and interface-based configuration model does not change in most implementations.
sections.eli5: A router already knows how to keep several separate maps, each with its own number. This idea simply says: use one map for each kind of address.

sections.title: Instance IDs per Address Family
sections.content:
Before this RFC the whole Instance ID space was used for IPv6 unicast. The RFC splits it into ranges, and the first value of each range is the default for that AF.

  • Instance IDs 0 to 31: IPv6 unicast
  • 32 to 63: IPv6 multicast
  • 64 to 95: IPv4 unicast
  • 96 to 127: IPv4 multicast
  • 128 to 255: unassigned

Each Instance ID implies a separate OSPFv3 instance with its own neighbor adjacencies, link state database, protocol data structures and shortest path first (SPF) computation. The existing LSAs that advertise IPv6 unicast prefixes can advertise prefixes of other AFs without modification, because each prefix carries its own length field. Prefixes that do not match the AF of an instance MUST NOT be used in that instance's route computation.

OSPFv3 still runs on top of IPv6 and uses IPv6 link-local addresses for its control packets, so IPv6 must be enabled on an OSPFv3 link even if the link takes part in no IPv6 AF.
sections.eli5: The numbers are split into blocks, like apartment floors: one floor for each kind of address. A router picks the floor, and everyone on that floor shares the same map.

sections.title: The AF-bit and Hello Processing
sections.content:
A router that does not know this specification but is configured with an Instance ID reserved for an AF could still join the SPF path and then black hole packets, through misconfiguration or a software downgrade. To prevent this, a new AF-bit is added to the OSPFv3 Options field. A router supporting AFs as described MUST set it in Hello packets, Database Description packets and LSAs.

Hello reception gains one check: a router that participates in an AF MUST discard Hello packets that have the AF-bit clear. The exception is the base IPv6 unicast AF, where the check MUST NOT be done, for backward compatibility. The existing V6-bit remains applicable only to the IPv6 unicast AF and is ignored in other AFs.

Because of this, a non-capable router using a reserved Instance ID forms no adjacency, and AFs can be deployed gradually without disturbing routing domains that contain non-capable routers. All the modifications apply only to AFs other than IPv6 unicast.
sections.eli5: Routers wear a badge to show they understand the new rules. A router that sees someone without the badge on the new floor politely refuses to team up with them.

sections.title: Next Hops, Forwarding Addresses and Virtual Links
sections.content:
For IPv4 unicast and multicast AFs it is desirable to have IPv4 next hops, for example so Reverse Path Forwarding lookups work for PIM. The link's IPv4 address is therefore placed in the first 32 bits of the "link local address" field of the IPv4 instance's Link-LSA, with the remaining bits set to zero. In the same way, the Forwarding Address of AS-external-LSAs and NSSA-LSAs MUST encode an IPv4 address in its first 32 bits for the IPv4 AFs, with the remaining bits zero.

Virtual links are not supported in AFs other than IPv6 unicast. Control packets on a virtual link are IPv6 packets that may cross several hops and need a global IPv6 address, which will not exist for the other AFs.
sections.eli5: The router writes the street address in the old IPv6 address box, using only the first part of it. Long-distance shortcuts only work for the original kind of address.

sections.title: MTU Handling in Database Description Packets
sections.content:
For non-IPv6 AFs, both the AF's MTU and the IPv6 MTU used for maximum OSPFv3 packet size must be considered. The Database Description packet MUST always carry the MTU of the advertised AF, so an IPv4 instance puts the IPv4 MTU in the Interface MTU field. A Database Description packet is rejected if its MTU is larger than the receiving interface's MTU for that AF.

Since the packet has only one MTU field, the RFC defines the M6-bit to say that the sender's IPv6 MTU differs from the AF's MTU. If the IPv6 and IPv4 MTUs differ, the M6-bit MUST be set for non-IPv6 AFs. If it is set, the IPv6 MTU comes from an optional IPv6 MTU TLV (type 17) in the link-local signaling block, or, when the TLV is absent, the IPv6 minimum of 1280 octets SHOULD be used. A router SHOULD NOT set the M6-bit if the two MTUs are the same.
sections.eli5: Two routers must agree how big a parcel can be before they trade. If the two kinds of roads allow different sizes, a flag tells the other router to check both.

sections.title: Security and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IPsec can provide OSPFv3 authentication and confidentiality as described in RFC 4552. When several OSPFv3 instances use the same interface they MUST all use the same Security Association, because SA selectors cannot select on header fields such as the Instance ID. Other security considerations are those of OSPFv3 itself.

IANA assigned the AF-bit from the OSPFv3 Options registry, the M6-bit from the DD Packet Flags registry and TLV type 17 for the IPv6 MTU TLV, and created the registry "OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values". Instance IDs 0 to 127 are assigned by this RFC; assigning anything in 128 to 255 requires a Standards Track RFC with an IANA Considerations section.
sections.eli5: All the maps on one wire have to use the same lock, because the lock cannot tell which map a message belongs to.
